course_title: Special Topics: Film and Media: Literatures, Genres, Media
subject: FILM
course_description: Rotating topics in film and media. May be repeated for credit when the topic varies.
course_notes: (Same as CPLT 202W 1) (Major Texts: Literature, Genres, Media: Radical Eco-Cinemas: Film and Ecological Being | This course will explore what it means to think ecologically and how cinema itself might think ecologically. We will consider questions like: How has the division between humans and non-humans shaped the modern world? How might humanity overcome these divisions to develop an ecological consciousness? And how might ecologically oriented cinemas complicate the human/nature divide and aid in expanding our identification with Earth Others?) (This class will provide an overview of several different branches of radical ecological thought including deep ecology, eco-feminism, and social ecology, and will read film as a medium in which human/nature relationships are embodied and contested in order to theorize complementary radical eco-cinemas. Radical ecologists identify the environmental crisis as being driven by a fundamental crisis in our relationship with the world, a relationship that - in the West - has been largely defined by domination. While traditional environmentalism seeks to address ecological challenges by working within existing social, political, and economic structures, radical ecology argues that those very structures are the root cause of both environmental destruction and the diminishment of human flourishing. It asks us to radically reflect on and rethink the way we perceive ourselves as ecological beings. In this vein, a radical eco-cinema may not only represent ecological themes, but might push the formal boundaries of cinema in order to express new and creative ways of being ecological.) (Class discussions and written assignments will focus on reading across texts and films comparatively and working through their attendant resonances and contestations. We will examine not only what film can show us about our relationship with the nonhuman world, but how it shows us these relationships, and how different "ways of seeing" affect our understanding of ourselves as ecological beings.) (We will focus on a range of texts within traditions of ecological thought and eco-criticism, critical theory, psychoanalysis, philosophy, and film theory. Film screenings may include Hayao Miyazake's Princess Mononoke (1997), Terrence Malick's Tree of Life (2011), and Paul Schrader's First Reformed (2017), amongst others.) (Students can expect to present on one film or text of their choosing, complete a short midterm exam, and compose two pieces of written work with the option of one being a video essay or creative project.)
